# Experimental design and data inventory {#sec-design} Before any statistics, we need to know exactly what was measured. In this chapter we download the study from recount3, build a clean sample sheet, and answer five questions that decide every later step: 1. Which samples and groups are there? 2. What is the biological replicate? 3. Is there a batch structure, and is it confounded with the groups? 4. What kind of library is it (paired or single, read length, strandedness)? 5. Which genome and annotation were used to produce the counts? ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} source("R/helpers.R") suppressPackageStartupMessages({ library(recount3) library(dplyr) }) ``` ::: ## Finding the study in recount3 recount3 [@wilks2021] has processed more than 8,000 human SRA studies with the same pipeline (Monorail, which aligns with STAR) and made gene, exon and junction counts available for each of them. `available_projects()` lists them all; we keep the one we need. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} proj <- recount3_project() proj ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| |project |organism |file_source |project_home |project_type | n_samples| |:----|:---------|:--------|:-----------|:----------------|:------------|---------:| |2239 |SRP166282 |human |sra |data_sources/sra |data_sources | 18|
::: ::: `create_rse()` downloads the gene-level counts and the sample metadata and returns a `RangedSummarizedExperiment`: a matrix of counts (genes in rows, sequencing runs in columns) bundled with gene annotation (`rowData`) and sample information (`colData`). `load_gene_rse()` in `R/helpers.R` calls it once and caches the result. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} rse <- load_gene_rse() rse ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> class: RangedSummarizedExperiment #> dim: 63856 18 #> metadata(8): time_created recount3_version ... annotation recount3_url #> assays(1): raw_counts #> rownames(63856): ENSG00000278704.1 ENSG00000277400.1 ... #> ENSG00000182484.15_PAR_Y ENSG00000227159.8_PAR_Y #> rowData names(10): source type ... havana_gene tag #> colnames(18): SRR8083864 SRR8083865 ... SRR8083876 SRR8083877 #> colData names(175): rail_id external_id ... #> recount_pred.curated.cell_line BigWigURL ``` ::: ::: ## What the submitters told us SRA metadata are free text written by the submitters, so it is worth reading them before trusting any automatic parsing. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} cd <- colData(rse) cat(strwrap(unique(cd$sra.study_title), 80), sep = "\n") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> ALS implicated protein TDP-43 sustains levels of STMN2 a mediator of motor #> neuron growth and repair ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} cat(strwrap(unique(cd$sra.library_construction_protocol), 80), sep = "\n") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> Total RNA was isolated from d10 MNs for RNA-Seq experiments and validation #> assays using Trizol LS (Invitrogen) according to manufacturer's instructions. #> 500μL were added per well of the 24-well cultures After RNA extraction, samples #> with RNA integrity numbers (RIN) above 7.5, determined by a bioAnalyzer, were #> used for library preparation. In brief, RNA sequencing libraries were generated #> from ~250ng of total RNA using the illumina TruSeq RNA kit v2, according to the #> manufacturer's directions. ``` ::: ::: The sample attributes are stored as `key;;value` pairs. Here is one sample: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} cd$sra.sample_attributes[1] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> [1] "cell type;;differentiated HUES3 into hMNs|date;;2013-01-10|genotype;;control|sirna type;;fluorescent|source_name;;fluorescent siRNA, differentiated HUES3 into hMNs" ``` ::: ::: `sample_table()` turns these strings into a tidy sample sheet. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} samples <- sample_table(rse) samples |> select(run, gsm, title, sirna, batch, date, read_pairs, mapped_pairs, unique_pct) |> FALSE) write.csv(samples, "results/sample_sheet.csv", row.names = FALSE) ``` ::: ## Groups and batches ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} with(samples, table(siRNA = sirna, batch = batch)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> batch #> siRNA B1 B2 #> none 1 2 #> fluorescent 1 2 #> scramble 2 4 #> TDP43 2 4 ``` ::: ::: There are four groups. TDP-43 siRNA is the treatment. Three kinds of control were sequenced: - **scramble siRNA**: a non-targeting siRNA delivered the same way. This is the right control for the knockdown, because it has the same transfection and the same exposure to an siRNA, and differs only in the target sequence. - **fluorescent siRNA**: a labelled non-targeting siRNA, typically used to monitor transfection. - **no siRNA**: untransfected cells. ::: {.callout-important} ## Our main contrast All differential analyses in this book compare **TDP-43 siRNA (n = 6)** against **scramble siRNA (n = 6)**. The two other controls are used in @sec-qc to check that transfection itself did not change the transcriptome more than the knockdown did. Choosing the contrast before seeing any result is part of the analysis plan, not a detail. ::: The submitters recorded two dates, which we treat as two batches (B1: 2013-01-10, B2: 2013-06-10). The read names in the SRA files agree: the first read of every run carries its flow cell ID, and the B1 runs we checked were sequenced on flow cell `D245NACXX` while the B2 runs were on `H0T47ADXX` or `H0T1LADXX`. ```bash # First read name of one B1 run and one B2 run (sra-tools, streamed from AWS) fastq-dump -X 1 -Z https://sra-pub-run-odp.s3.amazonaws.com/sra/SRR8083865/SRR8083865 | head -1 #> @SRR8083865.1 D245NACXX130417:3:1111:5807:75955 length=152 fastq-dump -X 1 -Z https://sra-pub-run-odp.s3.amazonaws.com/sra/SRR8083872/SRR8083872 | head -1 #> @SRR8083872.1 H0T47ADXX130625:2:1201:14704:28078 length=152 ``` Both groups of the main contrast are present in both batches (2 + 2 in B1, 4 + 4 in B2). That matters a lot: - If batch and condition were **confounded** (for example all knockdowns in B1 and all scrambles in B2), no statistical model could separate the knockdown effect from the batch effect. - Because the design is **balanced**, we can estimate the batch effect from the data and remove it from the comparison by adding `batch` to the model (`~ batch + condition`, @sec-de). ## What is the biological replicate? The *replicate* is the unit that is independently exposed to the treatment. It decides what our p-values mean. From the metadata: - All 18 samples come from **one cell line** (HUES3), differentiated into motor neurons. - Total RNA was extracted from "d10 MNs" grown in 24-well cultures (protocol text above). - Replicates are numbered rep1 to rep6 within each siRNA group, and each has its own GEO sample (GSM) and library. So a replicate here is a separately treated culture of the same cell line, processed in one of two batches. The metadata do not say whether the cultures came from separate differentiations; the paper's Methods are the place to check this before you publish anything based on these data. Two consequences follow: 1. Our statistics describe variability **between cultures of one cell line under this protocol**. They do not describe variability between people. A gene that responds to TDP-43 knockdown here may or may not respond in neurons from other donors. 2. If several "replicates" came from the same differentiation, they are not fully independent, and the p-values will be somewhat optimistic. This is a limitation to state in the report, not something we can fix in software. ::: {.callout-tip} Write down the replicate unit before you open the count matrix. For patient samples it is the person; for pseudobulk single-cell data it is the donor, never the cell; for cell lines it is the independent culture or differentiation. ::: ## Library type ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} cd <- colData(rse) data.frame( layout = unique(cd$sra.library_layout), platform = unique(cd$sra.platform_model), read_info = unique(gsub("count:[0-9]+,", "", cd$sra.read_info)) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|layout |platform |read_info | |:------|:-------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------| |paired |Illumina HiSeq 2000 |index:0,average:76,stdev:0|index:1,average:76,stdev:0 |
::: ::: - **Paired-end**, two reads (index 0 and index 1) of **76 bp** per fragment. This read length is what rMATS needs in @sec-rmats. - **Kit**: Illumina TruSeq RNA v2, a poly(A)-selection kit. As far as we know from the kit name it is *not* strand-specific, but a kit name in a metadata field is a claim, not a measurement. @sec-strand measures it. - **Depth**: between 12.3 and 57.3 million read pairs per run, with more than 94% uniquely mapped in every sample. ## Reference and annotation ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} metadata(rse)$annotation ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> [1] "gencode_v26" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} table(rowData(rse)$gene_type) |> sort(decreasing = TRUE) |> head(8) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> #> protein_coding processed_pseudogene lincRNA #> 22321 10812 7835 #> antisense unprocessed_pseudogene misc_RNA #> 5726 3343 2391 #> snRNA miRNA #> 2053 1892 ``` ::: ::: recount3 aligned all reads to **GRCh38** and summarised gene counts with **GENCODE release 26**. We use the same release everywhere in this book: for the gene counts, for deciding whether a splice junction is annotated (@sec-cryptic), and for the small alignment demo and rMATS run (@sec-strand, @sec-rmats). Gene identifiers carry a version suffix (`ENSG00000120948.15` for *TARDBP*), which is a quick way to check that two tables come from the same release. ::: {.callout-warning} ## One annotation per project GENCODE v26 corresponds to Ensembl 88. Gene models, gene IDs and even gene symbols change between releases. If counts come from one release and the junction or splicing annotation from another, "novel" junctions may only be novel to the older release, and gene IDs may fail to match. Pick one release and write it in the Methods. ::: ## From coverage to read counts recount3 does not count reads directly. It stores the **sum of base-level coverage** over each gene. To get numbers that behave like read counts, divide by the average mapped read length. For paired-end data that length covers both mates, so the result is close to a count of fragments. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} assay(rse, "counts") <- compute_read_counts(rse) counts_per_sample <- colSums(assay(rse, "counts")) summary(counts_per_sample / samples[colnames(rse), "mapped_pairs"]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> Min. 1st Qu. Median Mean 3rd Qu. Max. #> 0.8446 0.8789 0.8879 0.8916 0.9056 0.9295 ``` ::: ::: The gene counts add up to 84% to 93% of the mapped fragments, as expected, because some fragments fall in introns, between genes, or on more than one gene. ::: {.callout-warning} ## Do not use `transform_counts()` for DESeq2 recount3 also offers `transform_counts()`, which by default rescales every sample to the same total (40 million 100 bp reads). That is handy for browsing, but it removes the real differences in library size that DESeq2 and edgeR need to model. For differential analysis, use `compute_read_counts()` and let the DE method normalise. ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} saveRDS(rse, cache_path("rse_gene_counts.rds")) ``` ::: ## Data inventory | Item | Value | |---|---| | Study | SRA SRP166282, GEO GSE121569 [@klim2019] | | Cells | HUES3 human embryonic stem cells differentiated into motor neurons | | Groups used | TDP-43 siRNA (6), scramble siRNA (6); QC only: fluorescent siRNA (3), no siRNA (3) | | Replicate unit | separately treated culture of one cell line (see text) | | Batches | B1 (2013-01-10), B2 (2013-06-10), balanced across groups | | Library | TruSeq RNA v2 (poly(A)), paired-end 2 x 76 bp, Illumina HiSeq 2000 | | Strandedness | measured in @sec-strand | | Genome / annotation | GRCh38 / GENCODE v26 (recount3 code G026) | | Source of counts | recount3 gene and junction files, AWS Open Data mirror | | Downloaded | 2026-10-31 | ::: {.callout-tip} ## Check your understanding 1. Why is scramble siRNA, and not "no siRNA", the right control for the knockdown? 2. Imagine all knockdown samples had been sequenced in B1 and all scramble samples in B2. What could you still conclude? 3. A colleague says "we have 6 replicates, so our result holds for human motor neurons". What is wrong with that sentence? 4. Why should you not feed the output of `transform_counts()` to DESeq2? ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Answers 1. Scramble siRNA controls for transfection and for the presence of an siRNA. Only the target sequence differs, so the difference can be attributed to loss of TDP-43. 2. Almost nothing about the knockdown: any difference could be batch. Confounding cannot be fixed by modelling; it has to be avoided at the design stage. 3. The six replicates are cultures of one cell line. They capture culture-to-culture variability, not variability between people. 4. It rescales every sample to the same total, which hides real library size differences and distorts the mean-variance relationship that DESeq2 models. Use `compute_read_counts()` instead. ::: :::
